summary.text: Opens Chapter 1 by explaining that about a quarter of the world's population is infected with M. tuberculosis, that 5–10% develop disease, mostly within a few years, and that people living with HIV, contacts and the immunocompromised are therefore priority groups for preventive treatment once active TB is ruled out. It places programmatic management of preventive treatment within the End TB Strategy, with its target of 90% coverage by 2025, and notes that coverage remained low in 2018.

summary.text: Opens Chapter 2 on identifying populations that need TB preventive treatment, listing WHO's criteria for choosing target groups, such as high infection prevalence, high risk of progression and benefits outweighing harms. It sets out WHO's two broad risk categories: people at higher risk of progressing to disease, such as people living with HIV and certain clinical groups, and people more likely to be infected, such as household contacts and those in institutions or crowded settings.

summary.text: Notes that preventive treatment may be given case by case to people with diabetes, harmful alcohol use, underweight or smoking, and then explains why people living with HIV are a priority, since their TB risk is about 20 times higher and TB caused a third of HIV-related deaths in 2018. It restates WHO recommendations 1–4 on preventive treatment for adults, adolescents, infants and children living with HIV, adding that children aged 12 months and over should receive it regardless of contact history or antiretroviral therapy.

sections.extract: Несмотря на то что систематическое тестирование и лечение не рекомендованы людям с диабетом, злоупотребляющим алкоголем, дефицитом массы тела и табакокурильщикам, ПЛТ можно проводить представителям этих групп в индивидуальном порядке в целях снижения риска ТБ, особенно в случае повышенной вероятности неблагоприятного исхода при развитии ТБ или наличия множественных факторов риска, связанных с ТБ. summary.text: Discusses the limited evidence for preventive treatment in children living with HIV on antiretroviral therapy or after TB treatment, the case for treating HIV-exposed infants and linking prevention-of-mother-to-child-transmission services with TB programmes, and the higher risk of TB recurrence, often through reinfection, in people with HIV. It then explains that household contacts under five, and especially under two, face a high risk of rapid and severe disease, so preventive treatment is strongly recommended once TB is ruled out, while other household contacts should also be considered.

summary.text: Restates WHO recommendations 5–7 on preventive treatment for household contacts under five, those aged five and over, and selected high-risk contacts of multidrug-resistant TB. For MDR-TB contacts it advises individual decisions, notes that the evidence for any single regimen is limited (studies used six months of levofloxacin, alone or with ethambutol or ethionamide), and recommends confirming infection with a skin test or IGRA, firmly ruling out disease to avoid levofloxacin resistance and following contacts clinically for at least two years.

Lists practical steps for identifying target populations, from setting up a national technical working group and reviewing guidelines to a situation assessment, universal TPT coverage for people living with HIV and young child contacts, and pilot projects to find other groups.

При проведении АВС среди групп риска национальные программы должны рассматривать возможность включения услуг ПЛТ в пакет медицинской помощи в целях расширения охвата населения при минимуме дополнительных инвестиций и наоборот – в программах по оказанию ПЛТ следует предусмотреть возможности для предоставления лицам, которые соответствуют установленным критериям, услуг по диагностике и лечению

summary.text: Argues that national trials of TPT efficacy are unnecessary and recommends prioritising people likely to have been recently infected, while stressing that effective infection control is needed so that reinfection does not erode the benefit of TPT. Begins the section on reaching target groups, setting out how HIV services should systematically screen people living with HIV for TB symptoms and link them to TPT.

sections.extract: Проведение масштабных исследований для оценки эффективности режима ПЛТ не требуется, поскольку процесс, описанный в руководстве ВОЗ, включает в себя исчерпывающий анализ данных самых последних клинических исследований. Более того, проведение подобных исследований по конкретным странам или группам может замедлить процесс широкомасштабного внедрения услуг ПЛТ, что лишит уязвимые группы населения доступа к ПЛТ. 6.

summary.text: Explains why household contacts of people with TB are a priority group for TPT, citing high prevalence of TB infection and disease among them, including findings from the PHOENIx study of contacts of people with multidrug-resistant TB. Describes the health, economic and infection-control benefits of investigating and treating whole households, and links strong contact investigation to the commitment to give TPT to 24 million household contacts by 2022.

sections.extract: • Для других целевых групп национальные программы должны адаптировать услуги по скринингу на ТБ и ПЛТ к потребностям и возможностям существующей инфраструктуры здравоохранения. Этот подход должен предусматривать обеспечение оптимальных и комплексных услуг ПЛТ наряду с другими услугами здравоохранения и социального обеспечения. summary.text: Defines contact investigation as the systematic process of finding contacts of index TB patients, assessing them and giving either TB treatment or TPT, and calls for it to be a standard part of national TB efforts, strengthened where it exists and funded where it does not. Includes Figure 2.1, listing indicative cost items such as health-worker time, transport for workers and contacts, specimen transport, data tools like the WHO Prevent TB app, and recording and reporting.
